newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: TENNIS-MOYA A "MARKED MAN", SAYS SAMPRAS.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-MOYA A "MARKED MAN", SAYS SAMPRAS.

text.p: Spain's Carlos Moya arrived at the Australian Open two weeks ago as an up-and-coming youngster with the potential to create an upset.
According to Pete Sampras, who beat him in Sunday's men's final, he leaves Melbourne a "marked man".
The 20-year-old had won only two minor tournaments before entering his fifth Grand Slam tournament. His total career earnings were US$590,000 -- Sampras has earned $25 million.
After Sunday's final he had shot from 25 in the rankings to nine, almost doubled his earnings in one tournament, and became a marketable sporting pin-up.
It has been a remarkable performance but Sampras, who won his first Grand Slam title at the age of 19, said Moya's problems could be about to start.
"He's a bit of a marked man now. He's in the top 10, people are going to be gunning after him," said Sampras.
"That's something I experienced maybe winning the (U.S.) Open at 19, it's a little tough to cope with that.
"But I think he has a good head on his shoulders and I think he will just get better the more matches he'll play."
Moya has been the most high-profile Spaniard in Melbourne, although his compatriots Albert Costa and Felix Mantilla also tore their way through the tournament.
All started life as mere baseliners, used to thumping the ball back and forth across the slow red clay courts of their homeland.
In the past year or so they have realised clay courts are not the place to earn the money and the ranking points available to hardcourt and indoor players.
They started to practise, play and win on other surfaces, helping Moya to become the first Spaniard in an Australian Open final since 1969.
"The Spaniards are going to be around for a long time," said Sampras. "Especially when the clay court season comes along, they're going to be very, very tough to beat."

Moya's immediate problem is to decide where to celebrate when he gets back to Spain. "Most of them want me in Barcelona, others in Madrid, others in Majorca. I don't know what I'm going to be," he said.
After that he's going to keep practising, keep improving and aim for a place in the top five. The French Open, where he will start as a seed, is an obvious next target.
"But I'm not going to change. It can change my life, but not me," Moya said.
